builders.name: Dallas-Arbiter
builders.description: Dallas-Arbiter is the principal original branding/manufacturing entity used for the Fuzz Face founding record.

builders.name: Sola Sound
builders.description: Foundational British fuzz builder/OEM behind Tone Bender-family products and multiple branded versions.

builders.name: Electro-Harmonix
builders.description: Manufacturer behind the Big Muff family and numerous later variants/reissues.

builders.name: Ibanez / Hoshino
builders.description: Retail/brand lineage associated with Tube Screamer models; Maxon manufactured foundational Japanese examples.

builders.name: Maxon
builders.description: Manufacturer/designer lineage central to the OD808/Tube Screamer family.

builders.name: ProCo
builders.description: Manufacturer of the RAT family; founding model history begins in the late 1970s.

builders.name: Vox
builders.description: Brand that sold multiple Tone Bender-family products, including Sola Sound-built British MKII/MKIII products and Italian-made model V828.

builders.name: Rotosound
builders.description: British brand supplied with Sola Sound fuzz products, including multiple generations of the Rotosound Fuzz Box.

builders.name: Park
builders.description: Marshall-associated brand whose Fuzz Sound was supplied by Sola Sound in Tone Bender-family forms.

builders.name: Marshall
builders.description: Amplifier company whose early SupaFuzz was supplied by Sola Sound and later produced by Marshall itself.

builders.name: Carlsbro
builders.description: British amplifier/effects company with an early 1966 Fuzz-Tone and later Sola Sound-supplied fuzz products.

builders.name: D*A*M
builders.description: Boutique builder with an extensive Tone Bender / fuzz-focused catalog and documented reissues of classic designs.

builders.name: Basic Audio
builders.description: John Lyons' Fayetteville, West Virginia pedal company; began making pedals in 1998 and has a large fuzz-oriented catalog.

builders.name: Monsterpiece Fuzz
builders.description: One-person handmade boutique fuzz builder with a documented family of germanium and silicon fuzzes.

builders.name: Blackout Effectors
builders.description: Founded by Kyle Tompkins in Vancouver in 2008 and moved to Asheville, North Carolina in 2009.

builders.name: Stomp Under Foot
builders.description: Boutique builder specializing heavily in Big Muff and Tone Bender-family recreations plus original fuzz designs.

pedals.description: Foundational fuzz pedal with multiple enclosure, branding, color and transistor-technology changes across original British production.
A broader product family and genealogy than a single simple model; associated with multiple brands and OEM relationships.
A large family spanning multiple major generations, editions, countries and reissues.
Family anchored by the OD808 / TS808 lineage and followed by multiple Ibanez generations and later variants.
One of the defining compact distortion families, with Bud Box, Big Box, Small Box, RAT2 and later variations.
Sola Sound-branded three-transistor Tone Bender MKII. The same basic production lineage was supplied to several OEM brands.
Vox-branded British Tone Bender Professional MKII supplied by Sola Sound, with early and later cosmetic distinctions.
Vox-branded MKIII lineage supplied by Sola Sound; documented two-control, germanium three-control, Hastings and later silicon forms.
Sola Sound's later Tone Bender family, with early 'bendy' graphics and later 'Batman' graphics and changing internal technology over the 1970s.
Rotosound-branded fuzz product supplied by Sola Sound across multiple enclosure, control and circuit periods.
Park-branded Sola Sound fuzz product appearing in MKIII- and later MKIV-type forms.
Marshall-branded fuzz first supplied by Sola Sound, with production later taken over by Marshall.
Early 1966 wedge-shaped Carlsbro Fuzz-Tone followed by a later Sola Sound-supplied three-knob fuzz product.
Early Big Muff family commonly called the Triangle because of its three-knob layout; later reissued by EHX.
Major 1970s Big Muff family commonly called Ram's Head; numerous production variants.
Late-1970s op-amp Big Muff family; distinct from the transistor generations.
Russian branch of the Big Muff family including Red Army Overdrive, Civil War, Green Russian and Black Russian forms.
Ibanez-branded Tube Screamer derived from Maxon's OD808 production lineage; early and late board/construction details exist.
Ibanez 9-series Tube Screamer with important output/control changes and later component substitutions.
Power Series Tube Screamer with multiple production changes and later Taiwan-made examples.
Plastic Soundtank Tube Screamer produced in Taiwan; related closely to TS9 family.
Tone-Lok era Tube Screamer with HOT mode and Taiwan production.
Long-running successor in the RAT family; introduced with LED and switching changes.
RAT-family model with a distinct clipping arrangement and later reissues.
RAT-family variant with a distinct production identity; included as a model rather than a RAT revision.
Limited vintage-style RAT product documented by Pro Co.
Collector-named Small Box Whiteface production form.

distinguishers.description: ARBITER - ENGLAND branding is associated with early production.
DALLAS-ARBITER-ENGLAND branding appears after the corporate transition.
Input/output jack surround shape helps distinguish early enclosure generations.
Painted lettering is replaced by decal-style lettering around 1970.
CBS/Arbiter and Dallas Music Industries branding appear in later British production.
Original British Fuzz Face production includes a transition from germanium to silicon technology.
Triangle-associated graphics help identify early NYC Big Muff family examples.
Ram's Head graphics identify a major mid-1970s Big Muff family.
Op-Amp Big Muff is a distinct historical family and is identified by external/product context rather than a full circuit record.
Kit Rae's Big Muff numbering is researcher-assigned for identification and is not official EHX numbering.
Maxon OD808 and Ibanez TS808 belong to the same foundational Tube Screamer lineage but should remain separate brand/manufacturer records.
Bud Box is an identifying enclosure form for early RAT production.
RAT2 is a distinct model family within the RAT lineage.
Some MKII examples were converted from existing MK1.5 stock, retaining the earlier stripboard basis.
Early Vox MKII examples can retain graphics closely related to Sola Sound-branded units.
Silver Hammerite finish and tall silver-topped knobs are associated with later Vox MKII production.
Two-control MKIII examples are associated with the unusual 'treble and bass boost' version.
Germanium-transistor MKIII production is distinct from the earlier two-knob silicon MKIII and later silicon MKIII forms.
Hastings address stickers identify a short period of cast-enclosure MKIII examples associated with Vox Sound Ltd.
Early MKIV examples use informal 'bendy'/'spaghetti' graphics terminology among collectors.
Later MKIV examples use the informal 'Batman' logo style and omit the MKIV model designation from the graphics.
Three-knob Rotosound Fuzz Boxes identify the later MKIII-family production period.
Early Park MKIII examples have two controls and a misprinted control label.
Early Marshall SupaFuzz examples supplied by Sola Sound use angular enclosures.
The early 1966 Carlsbro Fuzz-Tone is associated with a blue wedge-shaped enclosure.
Later three-knob Carlsbro fuzz examples are documented as Sola Sound-supplied and closely related to the contemporary Park/Vox/Sola Sound MKIV family.
Triangle-family graphics and triangular control layout identify early Big Muff production.
Ram's Head nickname derives from enclosure graphics; multiple graphic editions exist.
Op-amp Big Muff can be distinguished at the family level from transistor Big Muffs by its op-amp-based design.
Black Russian production moved from large six-screw boxes to smaller four-screw boxes during its life.
Early TS808s use MP-D01201A board; useful alongside serial/date and external clues.
Later original TS808s use MP-D01201B board.
Black-label TS9 examples are associated with early original production; label and serial are useful identifiers.
Silver-label TS9s are associated with later original production, though reissues can look very similar.
TS10 architecture and board-mounted controls distinguish it from TS808/TS9 construction.
Plastic Soundtank housing is a strong external identifier for TS5.
Metal Tone-Lok enclosure and HOT switch identify TS7.
CE marking on later TS9 reissues helps distinguish them from some earlier original examples.
Bud Industries enclosure is the defining external feature of earliest RAT production.
Fringe RAT logo and Tone control identify early 1979 production.
White-fill RAT logo is the hallmark of the 1984 Small Box Whiteface.
Thin blackface RAT logo replaced Whiteface screen printing in 1986.
RAT2 designation and LED/switching changes identify the later standard family.

claims.claim_text: Fuzz Face first appeared in 1966.
claims.editorial_note: Foundational date; retain as approximate to avoid implying a precise day.

claims.claim_text: Early Fuzz Face examples carried Arbiter branding and later Dallas-Arbiter branding appeared after the corporate transition.
claims.editorial_note: Use branding as an external identifier.

claims.claim_text: Original British production transitioned from germanium to silicon technology.
claims.editorial_note: Technical distinction is retained because it is historically useful, not as a complete circuit record.

claims.claim_text: Big Muff researcher's version numbers are identification classifications rather than official EHX version numbers.
claims.editorial_note: Important editorial policy for the archive.

claims.claim_text: Maxon OD808 and the Ibanez TS808 are part of the foundational Tube Screamer lineage.
claims.editorial_note: Separate brand and manufacturing records should still be maintained.

claims.claim_text: The exact production quantity and date boundaries for early Bud Box RATs are disputed in secondary sources.
claims.editorial_note: Do not turn the disputed number into a hard fact.

claims.claim_text: Tone Bender is best treated as a family/genealogy rather than a single linear version ladder.
claims.editorial_note: This determines the database architecture.

claims.claim_text: The Tone Bender MK1.5 designation is a modern collector/research label, not a documented manufacturer designation.
claims.editorial_note: Keep 'MK1.5' explicitly marked as archival terminology.

claims.claim_text: Sola Sound manufactured the Professional MKII for its own brand and as an OEM product for other companies during 1966-1968.
claims.editorial_note: OEM relationships are central to Tone Bender genealogy.

claims.claim_text: Vox Tone Bender MKIII production included at least three materially different fuzz circuits under the same model designation.
claims.editorial_note: Strong example of why model name alone is insufficient.

claims.claim_text: Tone Bender MKIV production evolved from germanium-based early-1970s circuits toward later silicon technology during the 1970s.
claims.editorial_note: Technical distinction is retained only as version-identification evidence.

claims.claim_text: Rotosound Fuzz Box production used multiple circuits and control arrangements across its production life.
claims.editorial_note: Create production-period records rather than a single flat version.

claims.claim_text: Park Fuzz Sound is a rebranded Sola Sound product with MKIII- and later MKIV-related production forms.
claims.editorial_note: Model identity and OEM builder relationship must both be retained.

claims.claim_text: Marshall took over SupaFuzz production from Sola Sound in 1968.
claims.editorial_note: Manufacturer and manufacturing-location fields remain separate.

claims.claim_text: Carlsbro's early 1966 Fuzz-Tone and later Sola Sound-supplied three-knob fuzz should be treated as separate generations under one product name.
claims.editorial_note: Good example of a model with materially different production eras.

claims.claim_text: The Big Muff's commonly used version labels are researcher classifications, not official EHX identifiers.
claims.editorial_note: Keep official product names separate from archive generation IDs.

claims.claim_text: The Triangle Big Muff may have entered production by late 1969/1970 even though some sources historically used 1971 as the first production year.
claims.editorial_note: Use a date range/caveat rather than a single year.

claims.claim_text: The Ram's Head family includes multiple circuit variants and graphical editions.
claims.editorial_note: Version research must allow multiple variants within a generation.

claims.claim_text: The 1978 Op-Amp Big Muff was a distinct historical product family from the classic transistor Big Muff.
claims.editorial_note: Technical difference included only for historical identification.

claims.claim_text: Russian Big Muff production included Red Army Overdrive, Civil War, Green Russian and Black Russian forms.
claims.editorial_note: Model/generation relationships need explicit mapping.

claims.claim_text: The original TS808 and later TS9/TS10/TS5/TS7 products form a Tube Screamer family with multiple construction and production changes.
claims.editorial_note: Use product model records plus family relationships.

claims.claim_text: Original TS808 production used two board generations described as MP-D01201A and MP-D01201B.
claims.editorial_note: Treat board information as a technical distinguisher, not a complete circuit record.

claims.claim_text: Original TS9 and reissue TS9 can overlap visually; serial, label and date-code evidence can be necessary for identification.
claims.editorial_note: Public guide should warn that exterior appearance alone may be insufficient.

claims.claim_text: JHS's RAT timeline disputes the popular claim that exactly 12 Bud Box RAT pedals existed and documents 12 circuits in 11 pedals, including one double unit.
claims.editorial_note: Historical dispute should be preserved explicitly.

claims.claim_text: The 1984 Small Box Whiteface and 1986 Blackface RATs are primarily cosmetic production distinctions according to the cited research.
claims.editorial_note: Do not imply a circuit change when the evidence describes a cosmetic one.
